TaskFlow

Participant pack B · a three-minute conversation about a chore-app prototype

Thank you for agreeing to talk to us. TaskFlow is a student prototype of an Android app for people who share a home. You do not need an Android phone: this pack shows you the screens, and on the call we will look at them together. We are interested in your honest opinion, and there are no wrong answers. Anything you find confusing or missing is exactly what we want to hear.

WhereGoogle Meet video call. The link is in the invitation.
How longFive questions, about three minutes, plus a minute for consent.
Before the callPlease read page 2 (consent), then pages 3 and 4 (the screens and the cue card). Two minutes is enough.

What the app is

A chore board for people who share a home: three or four people and a handful of chores that repeat. It answers one question: whose turn is it, and has it been done? You sign in, open your household, and see three lists: YOURS, OTHERS and DONE THIS CYCLE. Tick a chore when it is done. If you are busy you can pass your turn to the next person, and it comes back to you next time round. There is a feed of what happened, and a per-person count of what has been done. On purpose there are no points, no rankings and no red warnings.

The example answers in this pack are written from the point of view of someone who lives with a partner or family. The questions are the same for everyone.

The screens we will look at

1. Sign inThe first screen. Email and password, or a link to create an account.
2. New householdA brand-new household is offered five suggested chores instead of an empty page.
3. The boardSplit into YOURS, OTHERS and DONE THIS CYCLE. Each row: what, how often, when, whose turn.
4. One choreTap a row: what done means, how often, Edit, History, and “Busy? Pass it on”.
5. Add a chore, step 1Name it, then say how often. Each option has a ? that explains it.
6. Add a chore, step 2Pick the number of days with one tap, then drag people into turn order.
7. ActivityThe household’s feed, in plain words.
8. What’s been doneA count per person for the week, month or three months. No ranking.

Cue card: things other people have said

Use this as a prompt, not a script. Pick the ones that ring true for your home, ignore the rest, and add your own.

Things people tend to like

  • Board is split by person, not by status. You see your chores first, then everyone else’s, then what is already done.
  • Anyone can tick anything. If you did the bins yourself, you tick it, and the app records who really did it.
  • “Busy? Pass it on.” One button hands your turn to the next person and says, in one sentence, that it comes back to you next time.
  • Undo for ten minutes after ticking something by mistake.
  • Five suggested chores for a new household (Trash, Bathroom, Kitchen floor, Recycling, Hallway vacuum). Rename or remove any.
  • Adding a chore is two short screens. Repeat intervals are big tap buttons (1, 2, 3 … 7, 14, 30 days). Each option has a ? that explains it.
  • “What done means” one agreed sentence per chore about what counts as finished, so it is not argued every time.
  • Overdue is amber, never red. No points, no streaks, no leaderboard, no shaming.
  • Quiet hours for reminders, and Light / Dark / System appearance.
  • Activity feed in plain words: “maya did a chore”, “sam joined the group”.

Things people find missing or awkward

  • Straight to Sign In. First screen is email + password. No way to peek inside or try a demo before making an account.
  • No Google or Apple sign-in. Register asks for username, email and password. No “forgot password” either.
  • “Sign in to your workspace” sounds like an office tool, not a home.
  • Everything is the same purple. No colour per chore or per person, so the board reads as a wall of text. Icons (bin, shower, plant) could help.
  • Adding a chore means typing the name every time. The five suggestions only appear when a household is first created, not later under “Add chore”.
  • No calendar. You cannot see the whole week or month in one glance.
  • No timeline of who is up next. The board shows today’s holder only, not “after me it is Sam, then Maya”.
  • Swipe on a row feels odd. It looks like it will delete the row, but the row springs back and passes the chore instead.
  • Settings are hidden in the three-dot menu (Quiet hours, Appearance, Join with a code).
  • History is two taps deep. Open a chore, then tap History.
  • No push notifications. Reminders come only from the phone’s own alarms.
  • No photos or notes on a chore (for example “the hoover bag is in the cupboard”).
  • Household admin is thin. You cannot remove a housemate who moved out, the creator cannot leave while others remain, and the household name cannot be edited.
  • “What’s been done” shows counts only, no chart, no “planned vs done”. Some want the comparison, others find counts fairer.

The questions you will be asked

Five questions, in this order, about half a minute each. Under each one is an example answer from another person, to show the depth we are after: specific, about your own home, and honest about what would not work. It is only an example. Agree, disagree, or say something completely different.

  1. Look at the board (screen 3) as if you had never seen the app. Do you understand what it is telling you and what to do next, or would someone have to show you? What exactly would need explaining?
    Example answerThe board I understand: my things, their things, done. Plain words, “Thursdays”, “every 3 days”, no jargon. What I would need showing: how a chore gets into OTHERS at all, who decided it is maya’s turn, and what “Add chore” will ask. My partner would not read the small grey lines, they would tap the box and hope. The board explains itself, the setup does not.
  2. The app wants an account before it shows anything, then offers five suggested chores. Setting it up in your home for real: who creates it, how do the others join, and where does it stall?
    Example answerI would set it up on a Sunday with the other two there, so we agree the list. The five suggestions turn a blank page into a conversation: “does recycling count as a chore?” Keep four, add Cooking. The stall is accounts: three emails, three passwords, one of us forgets theirs within a month, and there is no “forgot password”. A shared code that just works decides whether we use it at all.
  3. Think of your actual week. Which chores would you really put in, and where would the app cost more effort than a whiteboard or a group chat?
    Example answerKitchen daily, bathroom weekly, bins Thursday, laundry, the cat. Adding them once is fine, the day buttons are quick, and writing what “done” means stops the argument over whether wiping the counter counts. The cost is typing every new chore, and that suggestions appear only on day one. The app wins on memory, the whiteboard wins on being visible all day without opening anything.
  4. The board only shows who holds each chore right now, no calendar, no upcoming turns. When would you need to see further ahead, and what should that view look like?
    Example answerWhen someone is away. If my partner travels next week I need to see what lands on me, and today I would find out when it arrives. A month view with the fixed-day chores is enough, interval ones can say “around the 12th”. And show the order: me now, who next, who after. With three people it is short, but it kills the “I thought it was your turn” conversation.
  5. Deliberate choices: anyone can tick anything, passing gives the other person the credit, no scores, no red, no ranking. In your home, is that fairer, or does it let people hide?
    Example answerNo scores is right for us, we are not children, and a red badge would feel like being told off by a phone. Anyone can tick is good, real life is messy. Passing is where I hesitate: the coverer gets the credit, fine, but then “What’s been done” shows my partner did more and not how much was covering for me. Honest numbers, not the whole story. Add one line: “of which 2 were covering”.
